question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{9-5x}$ at the point where $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=9-5x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-5) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{9-5x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{9-5x}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{-5}{2\sqrt{9-5(1)}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{2\sqrt{4}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-5x+9}+4{x}^{3}$ at the point where $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Let $f(x)=\sqrt{-5x+9}.$ We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-5x+9.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-5) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{-5x+9}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{-5x+9}}+12x^{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{-5(1)+9}}+12(1)^{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}+12 \\  & =\frac{43}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
